summary: This is the first part of the Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) specification. It defines how to encrypt email messages and authenticate their senders for transfer over Internet mail. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: PEM adds encryption and message authentication to Internet mail without requiring changes to mail relays. It converts text to a standard form before protecting it so different mail systems can process the message. RFC 1421 is Historic.

questions: what is a mic in pem
what is a message integrity check
subtitle: The message-processing and encryption procedures defined for Privacy Enhanced Mail.

tldr.problem: Internet mail systems can change line endings and character representations while relaying a message. Encryption and integrity checks need a representation that survives those changes.
tldr.mechanism: Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) converts text to a canonical form, computes a message integrity check, optionally encrypts the text, and encodes protected content in printable characters. Header fields carry the algorithms, keys, and recipient information needed to process it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1421 is Historic and obsoletes RFC 1113. Its procedures were designed for RFC 822 text mail and are part of a related set of PEM documents.

today: RFC 1421 is Historic and obsoletes RFC 1113. It was written as the message-processing part of a related set that also addresses key management, algorithms, and key-management formats.

sections.title: Services and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1421 defines message encryption and authentication procedures for Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM). Its services are applied end to end between the sender and recipient at or above the user-agent level, so intermediate mail relays do not need special processing.

PEM provides confidentiality, originator authentication, message integrity, and, with asymmetric key management, non-repudiation of origin. Confidentiality is optional; the other listed services apply to PEM messages. This RFC covers RFC 822 text mail and does not address access control, replay prevention, or proof of receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: PEM protects a message between its sender and recipient while ordinary mail relays carry it. It can encrypt the content, and it checks who sent it and whether the protected text changed.

sections.title: Data Keys and Interchange Keys
sections.content:
PEM uses a Data Encrypting Key (DEK) for message encryption and, for some algorithms, for computing the message integrity check (MIC). The RFC recommends generating a DEK separately for each message.

An Interchange Key (IK) protects DEKs as they travel to recipients. With symmetric key management, sender and recipient share an IK. With asymmetric key management, the recipient's public component encrypts the DEK, while the sender's private component signs the MIC.
sections.plainLanguage: A fresh data key protects each message. A separate interchange key protects the data key so the intended recipient can recover it.

sections.title: Preparing Mail for Transfer
sections.content:
PEM starts with the message in its local character set and line format. It converts the text to a canonical form using ASCII and CR-LF line endings, then computes a MIC; ENCRYPTED messages also encrypt the canonical text.

For ENCRYPTED and MIC-ONLY messages, the resulting data is converted into printable characters so mail systems can carry it. The encoding represents 24 input bits with four characters from a 64-character set. Lines contain 64 characters except the final line, which may be shorter.
sections.plainLanguage: PEM first puts the message into a shared text form, then checks it and may encrypt it. It turns protected data into printable characters so mail systems can transfer it reliably.

sections.title: PEM Boundaries and Message Types
sections.content:
A PEM message is placed inside the mail body between boundary lines. Its encapsulated header carries control fields such as Proc-Type, Content-Domain, and, for encrypted messages, DEK-Info. Text outside the boundaries can provide annotations, and PEM messages can be nested.

The Proc-Type value identifies one of four types. ENCRYPTED includes confidentiality; MIC-ONLY includes integrity and authentication but no confidentiality; MIC-CLEAR leaves the text readable without PEM software; and CRL carries certificate revocation lists.
sections.plainLanguage: The boundary lines mark the PEM-protected part of a mail message. Its type says whether the text is encrypted, readable but integrity-protected, or carrying certificate revocation information.

sections.title: Forwarding and Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
An encrypted message cannot be forwarded unchanged to someone who lacks its DEK. Before forwarding, a user must reduce it to MIC-ONLY or MIC-CLEAR, preserving the original MIC, or encrypt it again for the new recipient.

A full PEM implementation is expected to send and receive ENCRYPTED, MIC-ONLY, and MIC-CLEAR messages, and receive CRL messages. It must support at least one of the symmetric and asymmetric key-management modes. The RFC also calls for some support for nested and annotated messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A recipient who forwards encrypted mail must make it readable to the next recipient or encrypt it again for them. A complete implementation handles the principal message types and at least one key-management mode.

items.label: Confidential
items.desc: Encrypts the encapsulated text and applies authentication and integrity.

items.label: Protected and encoded
items.desc: Applies authentication and integrity without confidentiality.

items.label: Readable text
items.desc: Applies authentication and integrity but omits printable encoding.

items.label: Revocation list
items.desc: Transfers certificate revocation lists without user text.
